narrative.what_i_did:
The operator opened with two bug reports from field-testing: no way to sign a family they had started, and the People tree still showing them as an org node even after they deleted their org. They asked me to find where the last session had left off and fix from there. I read the prior session.json first per the standing order — the previous carpenter shipped the family-mode substrate plus the StartFamilyModal founder UI plus PeopleTree v1 plus the IdentityChip rollout, and explicitly named the member-side ratify surface and the founder-to-member delivery leg as next-up cuts. That tracked one of the bugs but not the other, so I grounded against the actual code before assuming.

I ran the four gates green up front and then read StartFamilyModal, FamilyIdentitySections, peopleTreeLayout, OrgDeclarationSection, MembershipChainSheet, createMembership, openMemberRoster, officialsRoster, and inboxEnvelopeHandler. The family bug confirmed: the founder card was render-only with no path to push the envelope anywhere. The org-tree bug took longer to trace — PeopleTree's extractOrgs walks holdings for credential_type='membership' envelopes where the member is the operator. The org-self-declaration alone doesn't feed it; the actual feeders are officials rosters, open-member rosters, memberships the operator issued, and self-memberships the operator received. All four carry the operator's identity in their org_id leaf when the operator is the org. The Delete-this-organization affordance only dropped the self-declaration; every other artifact survived.

Before cutting I asked the operator three chip-form questions per PFOR-019 to pin scope: which family-sign gap, where the org-ness was lingering, and what specifically they had deleted. They answered founder-side send, People-tree-still-has-org-node, and Settings delete. That made both fixes concrete and bounded.

First commit (29b3c9e) — the org-delete cascade landed in OrgDeclarationSection. The new deleteOrgDeclaration collects every envelope id in holdings whose org_id leaf equals wallet.identity, adds the org-self-declaration's id to the set, calls wallet.unhold on each in a loop, then does one save+refresh for the whole batch. Memberships the operator holds from OTHER orgs stay untouched, family-units stay untouched, handshakes stay untouched. The unholdEnvelope prop is no longer used in OrgDeclarationSection so I removed it from the component's Props interface and the SettingsScreen prop pass-through. Same commit shipped the family send-affordance in FamilyIdentitySections — a Send-to-members button on each family card the operator founded that ships the envelope via Mycelium to every named non-founder member that has not signed yet.

The operator field-tested and reported back via screenshot: 'Seems to still be there.' I grounded honestly in what the screenshot actually showed — per peopleTreeLayout and PeopleTree, an org node renders with bg-violet-50 + border-violet-300 and a dashed violet edge, and the screenshot showed only peer-style chips with gradient identicons. The operator confirmed via chip-form: the suspect node was a handshake to a test peer ('TomTest'), not the deleted org. The cascade fix had actually worked; they picked Skip-cutting-until-we-confirm-a-real-bug.

Second commit (3df3542) — the operator asked for a delete button for people. I asked chip-form questions to pin scope (chat-thread-header location + handshake-plus-chat-history removal scope). WalletProvider gained a removePeerConnection callback that drops the handshake envelope via wallet.unhold AND clears the chat-thread Map entry for that peer in one atomic save+refresh; the useChatPersistence debounce picks up the shrunken Map and writes the smaller blob to IDB automatically. PeerThread's header got a small red Remove button to the right of the back-link and the peer name + badge cluster; tapping it surfaces a red-tinted confirm sheet below the header that spells out exactly what gets removed. On confirm the handler awaits removePeerConnection then calls onBack().

Third commit (04fa944) — the operator field-tested the family-send and reported two related bugs: 'Send to family button just lies and then reverts once you come back. No indication the message is pending but persistent. Original family starter can't sign but shows I haven't signed yet also.' I grounded in the signing path and found the actual root cause for the founder-unsigned bug: wallet.sign records the signature's signer as the active keypair pubkey, which for a rotated wallet differs from the genesis identity pubkey the family-unit member list stores. familySignatureProgress's direct pubkey match missed the rotated signature, so the founder appeared unsigned even though their wallet did sign. The fix lifted both familySignatureProgress and a new sibling predicate memberHasSigned to accept an optional keyAliases map; FamilyIdentitySections now passes {wallet.identity → wallet.keyHistory} so any key the operator has ever used counts as their signature. Backward-compatible — callers passing no aliases get the old behavior. Five new tests cover the rotated-wallet bridge.

The lying-status bug had a different root cause: the 'Sent to N members · they will sign and the count will climb' status text was component-local React state. Tab-switch unmounted FamilyIdentitySections, the state evaporated, and on return the button reverted to 'Send to N unsigned' with no trace of the prior send. The operator's complaint of 'no persistent pending indicator' was the honest diagnosis. Fix: remove the transient success text entirely and replace it with per-member persistent labels that are computed from envelope state every render — 'signed' in emerald when the member's pubkey (or alias) appears in the signers list, 'awaiting signature' in amber otherwise. Because they're derived from holdings, they survive navigation. The aggregate 'N of M signed' chip uses the same bridge. The button renamed to 'Send to N awaiting member(s)' to convey re-tappable safety. The failure path keeps its inline error message because a failed send needs operator action.

Final state across the session: four commits (three substantive cuts plus the comms checkpoint from the prior session.json), seven code files plus the manifest, all four gates green throughout — typecheck silent, lint silent, 323 of 323 tests in 11.37 seconds (gained 5 new tests across the session), build clean. The wallet's curation surfaces are now end-to-end honest: delete-org cascades, send-to-members has persistent state, remove-this-person works, founder-signed-state is correctly detected across key rotations.
narrative.whats_pending:
The family-mode arc still has the member-side ratify surface as its next-up cut. When a named member's wallet receives a family-unit envelope via Mycelium, the inbox surfaces it as a generic unknown envelope row today because routeFor does not recognize the family_unit credential_type yet. The cut would add envelope routing for family-unit envelopes plus a FamilyRatifyModal that lets the named member review the family, see who else is in it, and add their signature with one tap; the cosigned envelope rides back via Mycelium and the silent-absorb path absorbs it into the founder's holdings.

A known sibling-bug for the rotated-keys bridge: the keyAliases pattern only fixes the operator's OWN signature detection because we know the operator's keyHistory. For OTHER named members who rotate their keys after signing, the founder's wallet would still see them as unsigned. The fix would require either (a) the cosigned envelope to carry a succession-proof leaf disclosing the alias chain at sign time, or (b) the founder's wallet to learn each member's keyHistory through some out-of-band means (perhaps a separate succession-link envelope that members publish). Out of scope for this session; flag it for the next time a key-rotation surface comes up.

A second polish note on the just-shipped peer-remove cut: removePeerConnection only drops the handshake envelope the PeerThread holds a reference to. If the operator has multiple handshakes historically with the same peer pubkey (Tier P then later Tier R, or any retry path), the older ones could linger. A future polish would unhold ALL handshakes matching the peer pubkey in one go.

WalletProvider.tsx is now at 798 lines after the removePeerConnection addition — over the 400-line soft warn and one line under the 800-line hard limit. The next touch to that file must include an extraction. Natural candidates: the inbox-related subscriptions + handler wiring (pull out into useInboxSubscription), the chat-related subscriptions (pull out into useChatSubscription), or the peer-mutation callbacks (sendEnvelope + syncEnvelope + removePeerConnection + unholdEnvelope cluster into usePeerOps).

The tree-v2 family-rendering cut still waits — branching a family-unit node into its members under the operator's center node in PeopleTree. The substrate is already there (findFamilyUnitsForMember + readFamilyUnit + the new memberHasSigned bridge), only the layout-and-rendering layer is missing.

Add-birthday-now sibling cut for the operator's own missing-birthday pain point still waits. Same supplement-credential pattern the family-unit substrate established (a credential signed today carrying a backdated as_of leaf for the actual past date) solves it.

Five named open future cuts on the PeopleTree v1 maturation remain open: angular sector grouping by category, zoom + collapse, multi-hop expansion (friends of friends), org-chain walking via walkOrgChain, and tap-a-node-for-detail. Four substrate-side candidates from earlier sessions also remain: receiveSelfMembership orgSelfDecl-lookup centralization, JoinOrgModal proof-candidate finder extraction, Phase D charter-amendment chain, and the appcommander metadata cleanup chip.

Field-testing the four shipped affordances on the operator's actual phone (org-delete cascade, family-send with persistent labels, founder-signed detection across rotation, peer-remove) is worthwhile before pulling the next thread.
narrative.what_you_could_do_better:
One honest observation. The keyAliases bridge I shipped is one-sided: it fixes the operator's own signature detection (because we have wallet.keyHistory locally), but for any other named family member who rotates their keys after signing, the founder's wallet would still see them as unsigned. The wallet doesn't currently know remote peers' keyHistories. A proper fix would either embed a succession-proof leaf in the cosigned envelope at sign time, or have members publish a separate succession-link envelope that the founder can hold. I named this in whats_pending but I could have gone further and started the substrate for the one-sided fix to also cover the multi-sided case. I held off because the operator's immediate symptom was their OWN founder signature being missed, and the fix that solves that case keeps the surface area minimal.

A second honest note. I removed the transient success status text entirely rather than persisting it. The operator's complaint was that the status disappeared on navigation. The minimal-correct fix could have been to persist the status in a small IDB store keyed on (envelopeId, ownerId) — then the success message would survive navigation. I chose the more aggressive fix of replacing the transient text with derived-from-envelope-state per-member labels (signed / awaiting signature) because those labels are PERMANENTLY honest — they reflect what the envelope actually says. A persisted status text would still have the lifecycle problem of going stale when signatures arrive (the text says 'sent' but the count climbed without further updates). The derived labels never go stale because they're computed every render. Naming the seam in case the operator wants the explicit 'I just sent at HH:MM' breadcrumb for their own peace of mind.

Third, the WalletProvider.tsx 798-line state means the next touch to that file has to include an extraction. I noticed this during the test run but did not extract this session because the headroom was sufficient for the three cuts that landed and an extraction would have been a separate scope cut from the bugs the operator named. The whats_pending entry flags it.

Nothing else surfaced beyond the declared scope this session.
narrative.bigger_picture:
The bigger-picture teaching across this session is what 'derived state beats transient state' means at the operator-facing UI layer. Three of the four cuts followed the same pattern: replace something that lived in component-local React state with something derived from a persistent substrate (holdings, envelope signatures, chat-thread map). The org-delete cascade replaced the leaky 'just drop one envelope' affordance with a derive-from-holdings cleanup that touches every related artifact. The family-send labels replaced the lying transient status text with per-member signed/awaiting labels derived from envelope signatures. The peer-remove confirm sheet derives its blast-radius prose from the live wallet state. In each case the substrate is the source of truth and the surface is a read-only window onto it; component-local state is only used for ephemera like in-flight 'Sending…' indicators that have no meaning beyond the current click.

The second teaching is what key-history bridging buys for sovereign-identity wallets that survive rotation. A wallet that lasts decades will rotate keys many times — for compromise recovery, for hardware migration, for the routine practice of forward-secrecy-by-rotation. Each rotation produces a new active key while preserving the genesis identity as the stable handle. Every layer of the wallet that compares 'this signer is this person' needs a bridge: from the signing pubkey on a specific envelope back to the operator's stable identity. Today this bridge lives in wallet.keyHistory locally and is opt-in (callers must pass it). A future cut would lift the keyHistory bridge into a primitive that every signature-counting helper uses by default. The familyUnit.memberHasSigned + familySignatureProgress pair this session shipped is the first place that bridge has crossed into a feature module; the pattern will repeat for officials rosters, ratifications, open-member rosters, and any future credential whose authorship is checked against a stable identity rather than the moment-of-signing active key.

The broader thesis-level connection is the same Layer 4 framing every session keeps reinforcing. A sovereign identity wallet succeeds when the cryptographic substrate is invisible to anyone who is not already curious about it. The operator who tapped Send and saw the status disappear should not have to understand that React component-local state is unmounted on tab switch; they should see the wallet's honest current state of who has and has not signed. The operator who founded a family and rotated their keys should not have to understand that schnorr signatures bind to the active key while attestations bind to the genesis identity; they should see themselves as signed because they ARE signed. The prime directive applies: clarity beats cleverness, useful beats flashy, safe beats fast. Every honest-verb cut moves the wallet a little closer to feeling like a wallet, not like a window into the cryptography.

feedback_to_appcommander: Five patterns from this session worth lifting into the skeleton. First, the cascade-delete pattern for compound identity claims. Second, the founder-initiates-and-substrate-absorbs pattern the family-send button uses. Third, the symmetric-curation-affordance principle — for every Add path in a sovereign-identity wallet there should be a matching Remove path at the same level of the substrate. Fourth, the derived-state-beats-transient-state principle the family persistent labels established — when a UI element claims a state, that state should be derivable from the persistent substrate (holdings, envelope signatures, IDB-persisted maps), not from component-local React state that evaporates on tab switch. The transient state is fine for in-flight indicators ('Sending…') but never for state the operator expects to survive navigation. Fifth, the key-history bridge pattern. A sovereign-identity wallet that survives rotation needs every signature-counting helper to accept an aliases map that bridges from a stable identity pubkey to the keyHistory it has rotated through. familyUnit.ts is the first feature module to ship this bridge; future signature-counting features (officials rosters' countRatifications, openMemberRoster verification, any future credential whose authorship is checked against a stable identity) should adopt the same pattern. Probably worth a doctrine note: when shipping a signature-counting helper, the API should accept the keyAliases bridge from day one. Also worth lifting into the skeleton's CLAUDE.md the GROUNDING GATE win from this session — when an operator reports a persistent bug but the code's own rendering rules say the bug should be gone, the right move is to ground in the screenshot evidence honestly and ask the operator to confirm rather than speculatively cutting code. The chip-form questions doctrine paired with the verify-don't-trust gate produced a clean 'the bug is actually fixed' outcome that would have wasted a session if I had jumped straight to a speculative defensive filter.
